title: Evaluating LLMs Under Production Parity: A Replay Pipeline for Safe Model Swapping in Conversational Agents
gist: A production conversational-agent operator replayed 20 curated real sessions through 8 candidate LLMs (GPT-4.1/5/5.4 families, Gemini 2.5 Flash, GPT-OSS-120B, Kimi-K2.5) under full prompt/tool/memory parity, approving only GPT-5.4 mini, GPT-5.4 nano and Kimi-K2.5. The headline finding is methodological: three models scored above 79% on the weighted Final Score yet were rejected solely by a separate eliminatory Hallucination Rate gate, and run-by-run recalculation showed two of those rejections were statistical ties rather than structural failures.

themes.theme: Why production-parity replay, and how it works

insights.claim: Model providers ship new families every few months and retire prior ones quickly without preserving cost, latency or success rate, so any team running a conversational agent in production faces a recurring forced re-qualification cost.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Model-swap validation is a permanent recurring opex line for AI application companies, not a one-off — a tailwind for eval tooling and observability vendors.
insights.quote: Providers release new model families every few months and discontinue previous ones within short timeframes, without necessarily preserving the same cost, latency, or success rate.

insights.claim: Public LLM benchmarks measure models against generic answer keys and cannot answer whether a new model behaves like the one already validated inside a specific product's skills, tools, tone and transactional flows.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Leaderboard rank is a weak purchase signal for production buyers; expect enterprise spend to shift toward private, replay-based evaluation harnesses.
insights.quote: Public benchmarks don't answer that. They measure the model against generic answer keys, not against your product's behavior

insights.claim: Separating declarative agent behavior (a YAML Skill) from model decision-making and exposing integrations as Python Action tool-calls is what makes swapping the underlying LLM possible without touching business logic.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Architectures with this separation turn model choice into a procurement decision, commoditizing the model layer and compressing provider pricing power.
insights.quote: This separation allows swapping the underlying model without changing the instance's business logic.

insights.claim: A valid model-swap test re-executes only the LLM's per-turn decision inside a reconstructed context — real memory and timestamps in the system prompt, the baseline's initial tools and messages, tool surfaces rebuilt on every Skill switch, history filtered after agent transfers, same termination rule — so performance deltas are attributable to the model alone.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: A reusable blueprint for anyone underwriting an AI vendor's 'we upgraded the model' claim: ask what was held constant.
insights.quote: it is literally the same prompt validated in production, not a simplified version for research
insights.locator: On top of this foundation, the test follows three invariants

insights.claim: Replay evaluation is not prompt injection because neither the reference script nor the expected response ever enters the candidate's prompt as an instruction — the candidate sees only the informational context it would have had in production.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Guards against the most common way in-house eval results get inflated; a diligence question to put to any vendor-published eval.
insights.locator: It's worth emphasizing that this is not prompt injection

insights.claim: Tool execution is the one place production fidelity must deliberately be broken: live execution would cause real irreversible effects on customer systems and would depend on current rather than historical system state, so matching calls receive the real recorded historical response and divergent calls receive a simulated failure that explicitly does not claim success.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Explains why agent evaluation cannot simply mirror production traffic — a durable technical moat for whoever builds credible agent-replay infrastructure.
insights.quote: It would be neither safe nor reproducible to actually cancel a policy during a test
insights.locator: There is a single point where fidelity is deliberately broken

insights.claim: Capping tool-call recursion at five per turn (MAX_TOOL_CALL_RECURSION = 5) plus a non-success simulated failure response prevents a single divergent tool call from degenerating into a loop within the same turn.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Runaway tool loops are a direct token-cost blowup risk in agent deployments; hard recursion caps are cheap insurance to look for in any agent stack.

themes.theme: Metrics design and judge panel construction

insights.claim: A credible agent scorecard mixes deterministic metrics — Tool Calling Accuracy checking JSON validity, action existence, parameter typing and tool-sequence equivalence, and a Task Completion Rate weighting step completion 45%, path efficiency 30% and closing satisfaction 25% — with non-deterministic LLM-as-a-Judge, semantic similarity and multi-round consistency scoring.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Concrete metric weights an investor can use to interrogate whether a startup's 'accuracy' claim measures task success or just format compliance.

insights.claim: Adding a tool-competence judge when a call diverges from the expected step prevents penalizing a model that solves the problem via a different but sensible path, correcting the rigidity of pure deterministic transcript comparison.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Naive trace-matching evals systematically understate newer models that reason to alternative valid paths — a source of false negatives in model-selection decisions.
insights.locator: When a tool diverges from the expected step

insights.claim: The judge model must have superior reasoning and a different architecture from the models under evaluation to mitigate self-preference bias, and score combination uses the median across judges for quality but the most severe classification found for hallucination detection.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Any eval where the judge shares an architecture with the candidate is compromised; asymmetric aggregation (median for quality, worst-case for safety) is the transferable design rule.
insights.quote: hallucination detection uses the most severe classification found among them, prioritizing safety over statistical convenience

insights.claim: GPT-4o mini serves only as a validation control rather than a candidate because Base 0 was generated by that model, which would make the comparison circular, while GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 act as the judge panel.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Circular-baseline contamination is an under-policed flaw in synthetic-data evals; its explicit exclusion is a marker of methodological seriousness.

themes.theme: Dataset curation as the binding constraint

insights.claim: Only 20 of 106 automatically customer-approved synthetic sessions survived manual turn-by-turn review against skill routing, system-prompt adherence, message sequencing and tool-call correctness — an 81% cull showing automatic approval is a necessary but not sufficient quality condition.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Golden datasets are scarcer and more expensive than headline session counts imply; the labeling bottleneck, not the model, gates enterprise agent rollout.
insights.quote: The reduction is not a loss of coverage — it ensures that the studied baseline dataset is reliable enough that the research won't reproduce noise.

insights.claim: The surviving reference corpus spans four service instances averaging 7.85 user turns per session (max 33) and 10.5 tool calls per session (max 32), meaning realistic agent evaluation targets long multi-tool trajectories, not single-turn Q&A.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Per-session token and tool-call volume of this size is what drives real agent unit economics — model list price per token alone underprices the workload.

insights.claim: PII in the baseline corpus is replaced with fictitious but structurally valid values — CPF and CNPJ numbers carrying correct check digits, substituted deterministically within each session — so narrative coherence survives anonymization without reintroducing original data.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: A practical pattern for regulated-industry AI evaluation where raw customer conversations cannot be reused; relevant to compliance-constrained deployments.

themes.theme: Results: who passed and who failed

insights.claim: Of eight candidate models, only GPT-5.4 mini (86.4% Final Score, 92.5% Pass Rate, 0.9% overall hallucination), GPT-5.4 nano (83.1%, 73.3%, 2.0%) and Kimi-K2.5 (80.0%, 77.0%, 0.0% hallucination) met production approval criteria.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: An open-weight model (Kimi-K2.5) clearing the same production gate as frontier proprietary minis is direct evidence of closed-model pricing pressure in agent workloads.

insights.claim: Kimi-K2.5 was the only model in the evaluation to record a 0.0% overall hallucination rate, beating every proprietary GPT and Gemini candidate on that dimension despite ranking below several of them on composite Final Score.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Open-weight models can win on the safety dimension that actually decides deployment, not just on price — a real substitution threat to proprietary API revenue.

insights.claim: GPT-OSS-120B collapsed in production replay with a 64.9% Final Score and only 10.6% Pass Rate because in 87% of sessions neither a tool call nor a text response could be identified, a consequence of its native Harmony format being incompatible with the pipeline's chat-completions standard.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Interface/format incompatibility, not model capability, can zero out an otherwise viable open-weight option — integration surface is a real moat for incumbent API formats.
insights.quote: in 87% of sessions, neither a tool call nor a text response was identified, due to the Harmony format

insights.claim: GPT-5 mini was the only model to register a critical hallucination occurrence (1.6% critical, 3.2% overall) alongside the lowest Pass Rate of the GPT-5 tier at 62.9%.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: A single critical hallucination is disqualifying under a hard-gate policy regardless of score — model-tier naming does not predict safety behavior.

insights.claim: Each model family fails in its own characteristic way even behind the same interface: GPT families most commonly choose the wrong tool (a judgment error, not a formatting failure), Gemini 2.5 Flash returns text where an action was required, Kimi-K2.5's technical failures were 100% HTTP 429 rate limits, and GPT-OSS-120B produced unrecognized decisions.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Failure mode, not aggregate score, determines mitigation cost — rate limiting is a contract fix, wrong-tool judgment is a prompt/eval fix, format mismatch is an engineering fix.
insights.quote: Provider rate limiting, not reasoning (Kimi-K2.5): 100% of recorded technical failures are HTTP 429s.

insights.claim: Three models with Final Scores above 79% and competitive Pass Rates — Gemini 2.5 Flash (79.7%), GPT-4.1 nano (82.9%) and GPT-5 mini (79.2%) — were rejected solely for breaching the overall Hallucination Rate ceiling, a gate applied afterward and independently of the weighted average.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Composite scores materially mislead on deployability; rank order and approval decision diverge for a third of the field tested.

insights.claim: In agents that decide about real customers, safety criteria must be independent eliminatory filters rather than components diluted into a weighted average, because an average lets a serious failure be offset by good performance elsewhere and still yield a satisfactory score.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: The transferable governance rule for AI deployment policy — and the question to ask any vendor quoting a single blended quality number.
insights.quote: In agents that make decisions about real customers, safety criteria need to be independent filters, not just another component diluted into a weighted average.
insights.locator: In agents that make decisions about real customers

insights.claim: The full approval matrix requires Score at least 75%, Pass Rate at least 70%, zero critical hallucinations and overall hallucination at most 2%, with the Final Score itself weighted 50% quality, 20% normalized latency and 30% normalized cost under a 30-second per-turn latency cap.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: A concrete, copyable acceptance threshold set for enterprise agent model selection — quality is only half the weight, cost is nearly a third.

insights.claim: Across the five rejected models the determining factor in almost every case was the incidence of hallucinations rather than overall response quality, so a model exhibiting a critical hallucination should be rejected regardless of its performance on all other criteria.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Hallucination containment, not raw capability, is the gating variable for enterprise agent adoption — the bottleneck vendors must clear to unlock production spend.
insights.quote: If a model exhibits a critical hallucination, it must be rejected regardless of its performance on the other criteria.

insights.claim: Recalculating verdicts run by run rather than on the volume-weighted aggregate showed Gemini 2.5 Flash near a coin flip (47.2% approved vs 44.4% rejected) and GPT-5 mini tied at 33.3% in each category, meaning their rejections depend on the specific session sample rather than on structural inability.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Single-shot benchmark verdicts on probabilistic systems are noise-dominated; demand run-level distributions before writing off a model or a vendor.
insights.quote: A single aggregated verdict does not justify discarding a model.

insights.claim: GPT-OSS-120B never achieved approval in any single run, which is qualitatively stronger statistical evidence of a structural defect than an isolated aggregate rejection.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Distinguishing structural from sampling failure is the practical test for whether to abandon a model or re-test it — a decision rule with direct engineering budget consequences.

insights.claim: Even among approved models, run-level approval consistency varies widely — GPT-5.4 mini at 84.6% and Kimi-K2.5 at 80.0% hold up, while GPT-5.4 nano is the least consolidated at 50.9%.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Approval is not binary reliability: a model that passes only half its runs carries hidden operational risk that an aggregate verdict hides.

themes.theme: Cost proxies mislead on true unit economics

insights.claim: Normalizing cost by token volume instead of dollars inverted the true ranking: GPT-5.4 mini earned the best normalized cost score (C_norm = 0.89) among all eight candidates while actually having the highest estimated cost per session at US$0.0925, roughly 5.3x GPT-5.4 nano's US$0.0173.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Token-efficiency metrics can point in the opposite direction from spend; model TCO comparisons must use contracted dollar prices, not token counts.
insights.quote: GPT-5.4 mini gets C_norm = 0.89, the best normalized cost score among the 8 candidates, but in practice has the highest estimated CPS — about 5.3× the cost of GPT-5.4 nano.

insights.claim: The cost inversion is driven by output-token list price (US$4.50 per million for GPT-5.4 mini versus US$1.25 for GPT-5.4 nano), not by the volume of tokens processed, making output pricing the dominant lever in agent unit economics.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Watch provider output-token pricing specifically — it, not input context or efficiency, sets margin for tool-heavy conversational deployments.

insights.claim: Estimated cost per session across the eight candidates spans nearly 6x, from GPT-4.1 nano at US$0.0158 to GPT-5.4 mini at US$0.0925, with Kimi-K2.5 at US$0.0520 and Gemini 2.5 Flash at US$0.0586 in between.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Sub-ten-cent per-session inference cost means model price is no longer the binding constraint for customer-service agents — reliability is.

insights.claim: Seven of the eight models ran through Azure AI Foundry — the entire OpenAI family plus open-weight GPT-OSS-120B and Kimi-K2.5 as Foundry catalog deployments — with only Gemini 2.5 Flash served via Google Cloud Vertex AI.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler model catalogs are becoming the default distribution channel even for Chinese open-weight models, concentrating gatekeeping power in Azure and Vertex.

insights.claim: Provider-specific friction is real engineering cost: Vertex AI required bidirectional translation of its own message and function-calling format, the Azure GPT-5 family refuses any temperature other than 1 and renames the output-token parameter, and GPT-OSS-120B's Harmony format was incompatible with the chat-completions standard.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Multi-provider abstraction layers carry ongoing maintenance cost that undercuts the 'swap in one line' pitch — relevant to routing-layer startup valuations.

insights.claim: GPT-5 family models operate under more restrictive Azure request quotas, forcing an adaptive concurrency cap of a maximum of 4 concurrent runs for those families while other models keep higher parallelism.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: Quota scarcity on newest model tiers is a throughput constraint that directly slows evaluation and rollout — a capacity signal worth tracking on frontier launches.

insights.claim: Unified routing reduces model swapping in most cases to changing a configuration name, but the divergent per-family failure patterns mean adopting LLM-swap does not remove the need for continuous per-family monitoring.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: The 'models are interchangeable commodities' thesis holds at the interface layer but breaks at the behavior layer — sustaining demand for eval and monitoring products.
insights.quote: Unified routing turns swapping models, in most cases, into swapping a configuration name.
insights.locator: LLM-swap is operationally simple, but not without monitoring

insights.claim: Planned follow-up work includes testing incremental capabilities such as improved function calling and extended context windows, expanding Base 0, resolving Kimi-K2.5's rate limiting, reincluding GPT-OSS-120B once Harmony-format extraction is complete, and replacing public list-price estimates with actually contracted cost.
insights.speaker: TechforHumans
insights.so_what: The named gaps flag where current agent evaluation is weakest today: real contracted pricing, long-context behavior and open-weight format support.
